abstract.p: The strength assessment of thick-walled composite cylinders under internal pressure requires consideration of the nonuniform stress distribution and the interaction of stress components arising from material orthotropy and axial restraint. Conventional assessments based primarily on circumferential stress may not adequately represent the multiaxial stress state governing failure initiation. This study investigates the elastic stress response and initial failure of an internally pressurized thick-walled cylinder made of Hexcel AS4/3501-6 carbon fiber/epoxy composite, with particular attention to the effects of wall thickness and three-dimensional stress interaction. An analytical formulation was developed using orthotropic elasticity under plane-strain conditions, and the radial, circumferential, and axial normal stresses were determined across the cylinder wall. The three-dimensional Tsai–Wu criterion was then applied to evaluate the combined influence of these stresses on failure initiation and to determine the allowable internal pressure. The calculations showed a nonuniform stress distribution, with the circumferential stress reaching its maximum at the inner surface and decreasing toward the outer wall. For the representative configuration, the maximum circumferential stress was approximately 188 MPa, while the axial stress remained nonzero because of the imposed axial constraint. Variations in wall thickness produced substantial changes in the stress distribution and the predicted failure response. The analysis also established a procedure for identifying the pressure at which the Tsai–Wu failure threshold is first reached. These findings clarify the role of orthotropic elasticity and multiaxial stress interaction in the strength assessment of pressurized composite cylinders. The analytical framework provides a basis for evaluating initial failure margins and examining the influence of wall thickness on structural pressure capacity.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: The structural integrity of cylindrical pressure vessels and piping systems is a major consideration in aerospace, oil and gas, chemical processing, and defense engineering, where pressurized components must sustain substantial mechanical loads while meeting stringent requirements for weight, reliability, and operational safety. Carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer (CFRP) composites are widely considered for such applications because of their high specific stiffness, high strength-to-weight ratio, and considerable flexibility in structural design. Their mechanical response, however, differs fundamentally from that of conventional isotropic materials. The directional dependence of elastic stiffness and strength produces nonuniform stress distributions under internal pressure, and failure may be governed by the combined action of several stress components rather than by the maximum value of an individual component. Accurate characterization of the stress field and the conditions governing failure initiation is therefore essential for assessing the pressure resistance of composite cylindrical structures [1], [2], [3].

The mechanical analysis of fiber-reinforced composites has been developed through several complementary theoretical approaches, including anisotropic elasticity, micromechanics, constitutive modeling, strength criteria, and laminated structural theories. Classical laminate theory and first-order and higher-order shear deformation theories provide established descriptions of the deformation and stress response of composite plates and shells, particularly when the effects of transverse shear deformation and laminate configuration are important. Micromechanical formulations, meanwhile, relate the effective material properties to the characteristics of the reinforcing fibers and surrounding matrix. Probabilistic approaches have also been introduced to account for uncertainties associated with constituent properties and the resulting variability in composite stiffness. These developments provide the theoretical basis for examining the mechanical behavior of composite structures, although their applicability depends on the structural geometry, material representation, and loading conditions under consideration [4], [5], [6], [7].

The response of composite cylindrical structures to internal and external pressure has received considerable attention in analytical, numerical, and experimental investigations. Previous studies have examined the effects of ply orientation, stacking sequence, fiber angle, elastic anisotropy, environmental conditions, and geometric parameters on stress distributions and failure initiation. The results have established that the reinforcement architecture can substantially alter the distribution of stresses and the location at which the first failure condition is reached [8], [9], [10]. Further investigations of filament-wound and thick-walled composite cylinders have addressed localized damage, through-thickness stress variations, and the sensitivity of structural strength to the arrangement and orientation of reinforcing fibers [11], [12]. Three-dimensional finite-element formulations and established composite failure criteria have also been employed to assess the strength of pressure vessels, including composite structures developed for high-pressure hydrogen storage. Such analyses have demonstrated the importance of accounting for the multiaxial stress state when evaluating structural performance under pressure [13], [14].

In addition to elastic stress analysis, the mechanical response of composite pressure-bearing structures may be influenced by loading history, manufacturing conditions, and material heterogeneity. Previous investigations have considered strain-rate dependence, viscoelastic deformation, residual stresses introduced during curing, variations in fiber volume fraction, and manufacturing defects such as voids and imperfect interfaces [15], [16], [17]. Thermoviscoelastic effects, orientation-dependent strength characteristics, and damage associated with impact or compressive loading have likewise been examined in the broader literature on composite materials [18], [19], [20], [21]. These studies indicate that the structural response of fiber-reinforced composites may involve mechanisms extending beyond instantaneous elastic deformation. Nevertheless, an elastic formulation remains useful for isolating the influence of material orthotropy, geometric configuration, and mechanical constraints on the stress state preceding initial failure. The present investigation adopts this restricted mechanical setting; environmental degradation, residual stresses, time-dependent material behavior, and progressive damage are not included in the governing model.

For a thick-walled orthotropic composite cylinder, the interaction between material directionality and structural constraints requires particular attention. Unlike a thin-walled approximation, which may neglect radial stress under suitable geometric and loading conditions, a thick-walled formulation must account for the variation of stress components across the cylinder wall. Furthermore, when axial deformation is constrained, the plane-strain condition introduces a nonzero axial stress even though the corresponding axial strain vanishes. The resulting stress state contains radial, circumferential, and axial normal components whose relative magnitudes depend on the orthotropic elastic properties and cylinder geometry. Assessing structural strength solely from the circumferential stress may therefore be insufficient, particularly when the material exhibits different tensile and compressive strengths along its principal directions. Although analytical elasticity solutions and composite failure criteria are well established, their combined application requires careful treatment of the constitutive assumptions, three-dimensional stress interaction, and the distinction between initial failure and subsequent structural collapse. In this context, the present study combines an analytical plane-strain formulation with the three-dimensional Tsai–Wu failure criterion to examine how the through-thickness stress distribution contributes to failure initiation under internal pressure. Particular attention is given to the influence of wall thickness on the predicted failure index and the pressure at which the initial failure threshold is reached. This approach provides a consistent basis for examining the relationship between orthotropic elastic response, multiaxial strength assessment, and the pressure capacity of composite cylindrical components.

Accordingly, the objective of this study is to investigate multiaxial stress interaction and failure initiation in a thick-walled cylinder manufactured from Hexcel AS4/3501-6 carbon fiber/epoxy composite and subjected to uniform internal pressure. The composite is represented as a homogeneous orthotropic continuum, and analytical expressions for radial displacement and the radial, circumferential, and axial normal stresses are obtained under plane-strain conditions. These stress components are subsequently incorporated into the three-dimensional Tsai–Wu criterion to evaluate the variation of the failure index across the cylinder wall and examine the influence of wall thickness on the predicted allowable pressure. The analysis focuses on the relationship between the nonuniform elastic stress field and the onset of material failure, rather than on the evolution of damage after the initial failure condition has been reached. The resulting formulation is intended to support the assessment of initial failure margins and the interpretation of wall-thickness effects in composite pressure-bearing structures. Its conclusions are limited to the assumed elastic material response, uniform internal loading, and constrained axial deformation; progressive failure, ultimate burst pressure, and long-term environmental durability remain outside the scope of the investigation.

CFRP cylinders commonly employ reinforcement arrangements containing circumferential and axial fiber orientations to resist the principal loads generated by internal pressure. Circumferential reinforcement primarily contributes to hoop stiffness and strength, whereas axial reinforcement supports longitudinal loading. The radial response is influenced more strongly by the matrix and interlaminar properties because reinforcement in the through-thickness direction is generally limited. Consequently, the effective elastic moduli, shear moduli, and Poisson's ratios may differ among the three principal directions, giving rise to orthotropic mechanical behavior [2].

In the present formulation, the individual composite plies are not modeled separately. Instead, the cylinder is treated as an equivalent homogeneous orthotropic continuum, with the collective influence of the reinforcement architecture represented by effective material constants. This representation permits analytical examination of the through-thickness stress field without explicitly resolving individual ply interfaces. It is therefore appropriate for the present continuum-level analysis, provided that the effective elastic properties adequately describe the composite configuration under consideration.

Under the plane-strain conditions adopted in the present analysis, the axial strain is constrained to zero, whereas the axial stress generally remains nonzero because of the constitutive interaction between the radial, circumferential, and axial directions. Consequently, the stress state of the orthotropic thick-walled cylinder cannot be adequately characterized by the radial and circumferential components alone. Although the applied loading is axisymmetric, the axial constraint introduces an additional normal stress that must be considered when evaluating the onset of material failure. The resulting three-dimensional normal stress state is evaluated using the Tsai–Wu failure criterion.

Failure assessment in fiber-reinforced composites requires consideration of the directional dependence of material strength and the interaction of simultaneously acting stress components. The maximum stress and maximum strain criteria evaluate individual stress or strain components against their corresponding allowable values. Although these criteria are useful for identifying component-wise strength limits, they do not explicitly account for interactions among different stress components. The Tsai–Wu criterion provides an alternative phenomenological formulation in which the combined stress state is represented by a quadratic function. Its linear terms distinguish between tensile and compressive strength limits, while its quadratic and cross-interaction terms account for the influence of multiaxial loading on the predicted failure threshold. The criterion is therefore suitable for examining initial failure in the orthotropic composite cylinder considered here, provided that the required strength parameters and interaction coefficients are appropriately specified.

The quadratic terms describe the contributions of the individual normal stresses, while the cross-interaction terms modify the predicted failure index according to the simultaneous action and relative signs of the stress components. Consequently, two stress states with similar circumferential stresses may produce different failure indices when their radial or axial stresses differ.

The Tsai–Wu criterion also differs from failure models that distinguish individual damage mechanisms. Whereas criteria such as Hashin and Puck are formulated to identify particular fiber- or matrix-related failure modes, the Tsai–Wu expression provides a single scalar measure of the combined stress state. Its continuous quadratic form is convenient for analytical calculations and numerical implementation. However, the resulting failure index does not identify the physical damage mechanism responsible for failure initiation. For the present study, the criterion is used to determine the onset-of-failure threshold rather than to classify individual damage modes or predict subsequent damage development.

The reported calculations showed that the circumferential stress was tensile and decreased substantially across the cylinder wall. For the reference configuration, its maximum value was approximately 188 MPa at the inner surface, decreasing to about 15 MPa near the outer surface. This pronounced variation is associated with the combined influence of cylinder geometry and the directional elastic stiffness of the composite. The circumferential-to-radial modulus ratio was:

The characteristic exponent, calculated from the effective stiffness coefficients, was approximately 3.703. This value reflects the pronounced difference between the radial and circumferential elastic responses of the equivalent orthotropic material.

Under the plane-strain condition, the axial strain was constrained to zero, while a nonzero axial stress developed through the orthotropic constitutive response. For the reference configuration, the axial stress at the inner surface was approximately -7.9 MPa, as obtained from the radial and circumferential stress components using Eq. (3). This contribution was retained in the three-dimensional Tsai–Wu failure assessment.

The calculated Tsai–Wu failure index varied from approximately -0.47849 at the inner surface to -0.00234 at the outer surface. The index increased with radial position but remained below the initial failure threshold throughout the cylinder wall. The negative values resulted from the combined contributions of the linear and quadratic terms in the Tsai–Wu criterion under the specified multiaxial stress state. Although the maximum circumferential stress occurred at the inner surface, the largest failure index at 50 MPa was obtained at the outer surface. This distinction indicates that the location of maximum circumferential stress does not necessarily coincide with the location of the maximum failure index at a given pressure.

This indicates that the reference stress state did not reach the initial failure condition according to the adopted Tsai–Wu criterion. It does not, however, establish an independently validated safety factor or ultimate pressure capacity. The quantitative failure assessment remains dependent on the material strength parameters and interaction coefficients used in the calculation.

These results indicate that the geometric ratio has a substantial influence on the local stress concentration in the pressure-bearing composite cylinder. A thicker wall generally provides a larger load-bearing section and reduces the circumferential stress under otherwise comparable conditions. The magnitude of this reduction, however, depends on the orthotropic stiffness parameters and the imposed boundary conditions.

The effect of wall thickness on initial failure was assessed through the corresponding Tsai–Wu failure-index distributions. Unlike a criterion based exclusively on circumferential stress, the three-dimensional formulation accounts for the simultaneous contributions of radial, circumferential, and axial stresses. Therefore, the radial location at which the failure index first reaches its critical value must be determined independently for each geometric configuration.

The smallest positive root satisfying the adopted failure criterion is then compared across the cylinder wall to identify the predicted critical internal pressure. This procedure provides a systematic means of determining the first attainment of the Tsai–Wu failure threshold without assuming in advance that failure must initiate at the location of maximum circumferential stress.

For the reference cylinder configuration, the critical internal pressure predicted by the three-dimensional Tsai–Wu criterion was 170.232 MPa. Initial failure was predicted at the inner surface, where the failure index first reached unity. At an internal pressure of 169 MPa, the maximum failure index was 0.96603, indicating that the predicted initial failure threshold had not yet been reached. The corresponding stress distributions and failure-index variation are presented in Figure 4.

sec.p: The comparison between the reference loading condition and the higher-pressure case illustrates the increasing importance of multiaxial stress interaction as the applied pressure approaches the predicted initial failure threshold. Since the stress components increase proportionally with pressure in the linear elastic formulation, their combined contributions to the Tsai–Wu index change through both first- and second-order pressure terms. The resulting failure response is therefore not necessarily proportional to the applied pressure.

From an engineering perspective, the analytical formulation provides a means of examining the relationship between wall thickness, orthotropic stiffness, multiaxial stress distribution, and initial failure capacity. Increasing wall thickness may reduce local stress concentrations and increase the predicted pressure required to reach the failure threshold, although this must be weighed against the additional structural mass. The present analysis does not establish an optimized cylinder design, since no formal mass–strength optimization was performed. Instead, it provides a mechanical basis for evaluating geometric alternatives and identifying the conditions under which the selected failure criterion predicts the onset of material failure.

The numerical results should be interpreted within the assumptions of homogeneous orthotropic elasticity, axisymmetric internal loading, and constrained axial deformation. The analysis does not account for individual ply failure, progressive damage, delamination, manufacturing defects, or ultimate burst pressure. These limitations are particularly relevant when extending the present analytical predictions to the design of practical composite pressure vessels.

The corresponding radial position identifies the location at which the selected Tsai–Wu criterion predicts initial failure. This location must be determined from the complete failure-index distribution and need not coincide with the position of maximum circumferential stress.

The calculation also shows why the initial failure pressure cannot be inferred from a single stress component. Even when the circumferential stress dominates the elastic stress field, the radial and axial stresses contribute to the failure index through their individual strength coefficients and interaction terms. The magnitude and sign of these contributions depend on the directional strength limits and the selected Tsai–Wu interaction coefficients.

The pressure obtained from this procedure represents the onset of failure according to the adopted phenomenological criterion. It does not describe the subsequent redistribution of stresses, the development of matrix cracking or fiber damage, or the ultimate burst pressure of the cylinder.

sec.title: 5.3. Engineering implications and limitations
sec.p: The analytical results illustrate the influence of orthotropic elasticity and wall thickness on the mechanical response of internally pressurized composite cylinders. In contrast to an isotropic material, the directional stiffnesses of the carbon/epoxy composite produce a stress distribution governed by the effective radial and circumferential elastic coefficients. The characteristic exponent in the analytical solution determines the variation of the normal stresses through the wall and therefore influences the stress combinations entering the failure criterion.

The geometric ratio
β 0
=
a b
provides a convenient parameter for examining the effect of wall thickness. For a fixed outer radius, increasing
β 0
reduces the wall thickness and changes the stress distribution under a prescribed internal pressure. The calculations presented in Section 4 indicated an increase in maximum circumferential stress as the wall became thinner. This trend is relevant to the preliminary sizing of composite pressure-bearing components, where structural mass must be considered alongside the pressure required to initiate material failure.

The three-dimensional failure assessment is particularly important when axial deformation is constrained. Although the axial strain vanishes under plane-strain conditions, the axial stress generally remains nonzero. Its contribution to the Tsai–Wu criterion depends on the axial tensile and compressive strength limits and the interaction coefficients involving the axial stress. Neglecting these contributions may alter the predicted initial failure pressure, even when the radial and circumferential stress distributions are accurately determined.

The analysis also identifies several limitations that must be considered when applying the results to practical composite pressure vessels. The cylinder was represented as a homogeneous orthotropic continuum, and the individual composite plies were not modeled explicitly. The formulation therefore does not resolve interlaminar stresses associated with discrete ply interfaces, local matrix cracking, fiber breakage, or delamination. Furthermore, the plane-strain approximation represents constrained axial deformation and does not necessarily describe the axial response of a finite-length pressure vessel with deformable end closures.

The predicted failure pressure is also sensitive to the directional strength parameters and the interaction coefficients adopted in the Tsai–Wu criterion. These coefficients require particular care when material data are transferred from unidirectional laminate tests to an equivalent orthotropic cylindrical structure. Without independent experimental characterization or a detailed laminate-level model, the calculated failure threshold should be interpreted as a prediction associated with the assumed material representation rather than a verified design allowable.

The present analytical framework is therefore most appropriate for examining elastic stress distributions, comparing geometric configurations, and assessing initial failure under the specified loading and constitutive assumptions. Independent finite-element or experimental comparisons would be required to establish its predictive accuracy for practical composite pressure vessels. Further extensions could incorporate explicit laminate architecture, alternative failure criteria, temperature-dependent properties, residual stresses, and progressive damage under static or cyclic loading.

sec.title: 6. Conclusions
sec.p: This study investigated the elastic stress response and failure initiation of an internally pressurized thick-walled cylinder made of Hexcel AS4/3501-6 carbon fiber/epoxy composite. An analytical formulation based on orthotropic elasticity under plane-strain conditions was combined with the three-dimensional Tsai–Wu failure criterion to examine the through-thickness stress distributions, the interaction among the radial, circumferential, and axial normal stresses, and the influence of wall thickness on the predicted failure response. The analytical stress solution was also checked against the prescribed pressure boundary conditions, the radial equilibrium equation, and the classical Lamé solution in the limiting case of equal effective radial and circumferential stiffnesses.

For the reference configuration with an inner-to-outer radius ratio of 0.5 and an internal pressure of 50 MPa, the maximum circumferential stress was 187.332 MPa at the inner surface and decreased to 14.303 MPa at the outer surface. The radial stress varied from -50 MPa to zero, while the axial stress changed from -7.943 MPa to 0.501 MPa across the cylinder wall. These results confirmed that the plane-strain constraint produced a nonzero axial stress and that the three normal stress components should be considered together in evaluating the failure response of the orthotropic cylinder. The calculated Tsai–Wu failure index increased from -0.47849 at the inner surface to -0.00234 at the outer surface, remaining below the initial failure threshold throughout the wall.

Wall thickness had a marked influence on the circumferential stress distribution. At an internal pressure of 50 MPa, increasing the inner-to-outer radius ratio from 0.4 to 0.7 increased the maximum circumferential stress from 185.554 MPa to 213.548 MPa. The corresponding failure-index distributions also varied with the geometric ratio, although the failure threshold was not reached under the investigated reference pressure. The results showed that the location of the maximum circumferential stress did not necessarily coincide with the location of the maximum failure index at a given pressure. Accordingly, the initial failure condition was determined by examining the complete stress-dependent failure index rather than by considering the circumferential stress alone.

For the reference cylinder, the predicted critical internal pressure was 170.232 MPa, with initial failure occurring at the inner surface according to the adopted three-dimensional Tsai–Wu criterion. At an applied pressure of 169 MPa, the maximum failure index was 0.96603, indicating that the predicted failure threshold had not yet been reached. These results demonstrate the importance of evaluating the pressure-dependent interaction among the three normal stresses when estimating the initial failure capacity of a thick-walled orthotropic cylinder. The analytical formulation provides a means of comparing geometric configurations and assessing the influence of wall thickness on the predicted pressure resistance.

The present findings are restricted to a homogeneous orthotropic material representation, linear elastic response, axisymmetric internal loading, and constrained axial deformation. The predicted critical pressure depends on the adopted directional strength limits and Tsai–Wu interaction coefficients and should not be interpreted as an experimentally verified burst pressure. Individual ply failure, interlaminar damage, progressive degradation, and manufacturing-induced residual stresses were not considered. Further investigations should examine the sensitivity of the predicted failure pressure to the assumed strength parameters and interaction coefficients and establish comparisons with independent numerical or experimental results. The inclusion of explicit laminate architecture, temperature and moisture effects, and progressive damage under static or cyclic loading would allow a more detailed assessment of composite cylinders under practical operating conditions.
